messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: factoring RStan, PyStan, etc.
parts:
The context of this is that we were discussing adding structured
mass matrices and I pointed out that for every change to
command-line Stan, there needs to be a corresponding reimplementation
in RStan and PyStan.

On 11/30/13, 12:00 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Shouldn't the interfaces be factored from these details?

Yes. As things stand now, anything in stan/gm/command.hpp
needs to be reimplemented in RStan and PyStan. So any
factorization of the code that will minimize the amount of
code that's directly implemented in the command-line code
would be a big help.

Also, anything with std::cout, std::cin, or std::cerr
hardcoded needs to be rewritten for RStan and PyStan.

Another option I've been considering is that we just have
RStan and PyStan call the command function in Stan directly.
There are two ways this could work:

Option 1. RStan and PyStan would:

* write data and inits to a file,
* convert config for the call into the appropriate format,
* call a new process to run models that writes output into files, and
* read the output back in.

This is what I did originally in the prototype, and then for
reasons that are now hazy to me, we switched gears to do a deeper
in-memory integration. In retrospect, I think this was a mistake.

Option 2: RStan and PyStan would call the command directly,
configuring it with the appropriate input, output and error
streams. If we do this, we'd need to be much more careful about
clean resource release (files and memory for now), because
R and Python are persistent processes, so it's very bad form
for a function they call to leak resources.

Option 2 is what we were aiming for with RStan, but work on
the command-line version of Stan has never complied. One of the
issues I remember is that holding onto C++ structures and making
them persistent, which isn't easy in R through Rcpp. That's
why the equivalent of the command-line bin/print is also completely
independently coded in RStan (or at least I think it is).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: sparse or structured mass matrices
parts:
[on stan-dev now]

On 11/30/13, 12:21 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> This would require a giant change to the HMC code, unless
> we move to a general sparse matrix sampler and even that would
> require a lot of work.

If by that you mean we'd need to refactor the matrix interfaces
to the samplers to something more general, then I agree. It's
going to be a lot of work however we do it.

Having structured matrices in the Stan modeling language is
a different, but related issue in terms of the linear algebra.
And it's absolutely critical if we want to build scalable
Gaussian processes along the line of Aki's GPStuff.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] factoring RStan, PyStan, etc.
parts:
Rather than ifdefs, I'd prefer to have reusable base classes or
richer arguments in order to use the language itself rather than
the preprocessor. It's more modular that way and hence makes
testing from within the language a lot easier, for a start.

For example, we have some things hardcoded for files or for std::cout
that should really be abstracted to deal directly with streams.

Michael's introduction of the mcmc_writer abstraction was intended
as a step in this direction, but it looks like we have further to go.

What I really think we need to do is abstract out the reusable bits
of command.hpp so they can be reused in R/Python/etc. --- that is, if
we don't go the route of just wrapping the command-line version of Stan
in the way that R2WinBUGS and R2jags do.

As far as I/O classes go, there's rarely a reason to make decisions statically
using template parameters or ifdefs as opposed to having more runtime
arguments.

- Bob

messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] factoring RStan, PyStan, etc.
parts:
On Sat, 2013-11-30 at 12:26 -0500, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Also, anything with std::cout, std::cin, or std::cerr
> hardcoded needs to be rewritten for RStan and PyStan.

In python having subprocesses that do both input and output can be a bit
challenging, at least if the sequence isn't known. I think more recent
versions (still in the python 2 series) handled this somewhat
better--maybe with the introduction of the subprocess module. ("Recent"
is at least a few years old).

So there might also be python version issues, if you don't want to
exclude "old" pythons. Old probably means < 2.4, since that is when
subprocess (http://docs.python.org/2/library/subprocess.html) was
introduced. As a point of reference, my system running a Debian that is
2 generations out of date still has python 2.5 (though it's possible I
got a backport).

From the motiving PEP (http://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0324/):
The subprocess module provides the following enhancements over
previous functions:
......
- A communicate() method, which makes it easy to send stdin data
and read stdout and stderr data, without risking deadlocks.
Most people are aware of the flow control issues involved with
child process communication, but not all have the patience or
skills to write a fully correct and deadlock-free select loop.
This means that many Python applications contain race
conditions. A communicate() method in the standard library
solves this problem.

It is definitely possible to hold onto C++ structures in R; I assume the
present code does because you can reuse models without recompiling them.
If stan ran in a separate process would that be possible?

I'm not sure if the proposal contemplates exposing the command line
invocation of stan to the R or python users; FWIW such a system seems a
bit klunky to me, although it's clearly more robust against interface
changes.

Ross Boylan

> and read stdout and stderr data, without risking deadlocks.
> Most people are aware of the flow control issues involved with
> child process communication, but not all have the patience or
> skills to write a fully correct and deadlock-free select loop.
> This means that many Python applications contain race
> conditions. A communicate() method in the standard library
> solves this problem.
>
> It is definitely possible to hold onto C++ structures in R; I assume the
> present code does because you can reuse models without recompiling them.

Just models. The samples themselves are translated back into R
structures because there's not an easy way to make C++ structures
persistent. I don't know how important that is, but I think that
was the main design consideration.

> If stan ran in a separate process would that be possible?
>
> I'm not sure if the proposal contemplates exposing the command line
> invocation of stan to the R or python users; FWIW such a system seems a
> bit klunky to me, although it's clearly more robust against interface
> changes.

You could still wrap the command-line calls so the interface
from the R side wouldn't change, though that would mean that RStan
would need to change to keep up with CmdStan, which is our "reference"
implementation insofar as it's what most of our developers use.

- Bob

Might there also be some middle way? Could we use sockets or something to pass
data between Python/R and C++? The maintainability problem isn't with calling
C++ code from Python or R per se, it's all the additional C++ plumbing (shared
by pystan and rstan) to construct the sampler arguments and hold the results.

re: memory. PyStan is creating copies of the data anyway in order to do parallel
sampling (which I think should be the default).

Best,

-a

Allen: You're driving the PyStan bus, so it's
really up to you at this point!

You could pass a socket address for reading to Stan rather
than a file name. I'm not sure what the support is in C++
or Boost for this --- if it's as easy as in Java, it shouldn't
be a problem to generalize our file arguments to sockets.
And ideally, we could even do HTTP to read web-served files;
that's also trivial in Java, but I have no experience doing it in C++.

- Bob
